newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia property index up 2.66 pct on review news.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia property index up 2.66 pct on review news.

text.p: Malaysian high-end property shares made strong gains on Monday as investors weighed in after the government announced that it may review property purchase restrictions on foreigners, analysts said.
At 0415 GMT, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's Property Index rose 53.87 points or 2.66 percent to 2,079.21, the strongest gain among the main indices of the stock market.
In comparison, the blue-chip Composite Index was up 20.95 points or 2.09 percent to 1,022.50.
At 0415 GMT, shares of Country Heights were 35 cents higher at 9.95 ringgit, Bandar Raya gained 20 cents to 3.06 and Land & General were up 13 cents to 2.88.
Sunrise Bhd was up 20 cents to 5.20.
Commercial property stocks IGB Corp Bhd gained 8.0 cents to 2.52 and Malaysian Resources Corp Bhd MRCB.KL was up 20 cents to 6.30.
Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Friday the government was considering allowing foreigners to buy commercial and residential property within city limits. But he did not give details.

Said Thong & Kay Hian on Monday: "As we await further details for an assessment of the impact on the property sector, it can be deduced that the immediate beneficiary of the revision will be developers of prime commercial property and high-end condominiums."
Analysts said the government was reviewing the curbs on foreign buying of properties due to concerns over a property glut, especially in the capital city.
"The easing of the restriction on foreign ownership of property is an apparent move by the government to revive Malaysia's flagging property industry," said Jupiter Securities in a research note.

Malaysia imposed restrictions on foreign property buyers in 1995 to curb property speculation. These include allowing acquisitions of properties priced at 250,000 ringgit and above and a 100,000 ringgit levy on all purchases.
There was speculation that the government may do away with the 100,000 ringgit levy.
But analysts said while the government's move was lauded, foreigners may be worried that they are being let in when property prices may ease due to oversupply.
"If the government wants to open up office space because there's a glut, foreigners may want to wait for prices to soften," said Wong Yee Hui, senior research manager at Merrill Lynch.
He said more details needed to be released before actual impact on the property market could be accurately gauged.
Added Jupiter Securities: "The move although is positive ... whether it will translate into actual buying and revive the property industry is not immediately known".
